PAPER: BIBLIOMETRIC RESEARCH Published Online: October 17, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multirev.2026239 Mapping two decades of extradition-related publications: A Scopus-based bibliometric analysis Faizul Aswad Masria | Rohaida Nordina | Muhamad Helmi Md Saida aFaculty of Law, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia (UKM), Bangi, Malaysia. Abstract Extradition is an important aspect of international legal cooperation, allowing countries to surrender individuals for prosecution or punishment across borders. Despite its significance, there has been limited systematic mapping of extradition-related scholarship. This study addresses that gap by conducting a bibliometric analysis of publications between 2004–2024 to identify publication trends, leading contributors, highly cited works, and the thematic development. The dataset was compiled from the Scopus database, where 837 documents were identified following clear inclusion and exclusion criteria. Analysis used Scopus’s Analyze Results, Harzing’s Publish or Perish, and VOSviewer to generate citation metrics and keyword co-occurrence mapping, following a four-step bibliometric methodology and the PRISMA framework. Among the key findings are the following: steady growth in publications with a marked surge after the 2019 anti-extradition bill protests in Hong Kong; journal articles accounted for most publications (60.69%), followed by book chapters (21.39%); Hong Kong was the most productive contributor with 156 publications, while the United Kingdom (122) and the United States (117) followed; influential works include Schabas’s “Genocide in International Law: The Crime of Crimes”, “Hong Kong’s summer of uprising: From anti-extradition to anti-authoritarian protests” by Lee and his collaborators, and Roht- Arriaza’s “The Pinochet Effect: Transnational Justice in the Age of Human Rights”; and six thematic clusters were identified, spanning extradition law, human rights, and the European Arrest Warrant, alongside emerging themes in global governance and political activism. This study clarifies the intellectual foundations, geographic distribution, and thematic development of extradition research. The findings underline Hong Kong’s dominance and reveal gaps in representation from other regions. Future work should broaden database coverage and adopt interdisciplinary approaches to foster a more inclusive scholarly discourse. Overall, the results expand understanding of extradition scholarship and its intersections with law, politics, and human rights. Keywords: citation analysis, international law, keyword co-occurrence analysis, research trends, scientometrics 1. Introduction Extradition is a vital tool of international criminal law, allowing a country to surrender persons to another country for prosecution or punishment on the basis of domestic law, a formal agreement, reciprocity, or comity (Bassiouni, 2014; Shearer, 1971; Starke, 1989). It is one of the bases of international legal cooperation, specifically concerning transnational crime, corruption, terrorism, and money laundering (Panggabean et al., 2025). Extradition differs from deportation, which is an immigration process through which a country removes an individual from its territory. Deportation is typically carried out for reasons such as unlawful entry or when the individual is deemed to pose a threat to public order or national security, and it generally prohibits the person from returning (Kiani & Purkhaghan, 2017). In recent years, extradition has received increasing amounts of scholarly attention, particularly in light of legal reforms and social movements (Chan, 2022). One recent example is the 2019 anti-extradition protests in Hong Kong, the biggest protest in the history of the city. The protests were prompted by a proposed bill that would have allowed the transfer of individuals to mainland China and other jurisdictions without formal extradition agreements, raising public concern about the independence and fairness of the legal process in those jurisdictions (Chan, 2022; Wang, 2023). A survey of academic databases suggests an increasing number of publications on diverse elements of these protests and their broader ramifications for extradition law, governance, and human rights. Such initiatives have expanded the scope of extradition beyond legal considerations, making it a subject of broader societal, political, and human rights discussions. However, despite this increasing interest, the literature on extradition is split across disciplines, and while there are some great contributions, there is no synoptic overview of how the field has evolved, who the main contributors are, and where there are still gaps in the analysis. This is the reason for the use of bibliometric analysis, which is a systematic study for mapping research trends, intellectual structures, and scholarly impact (Passas, 2024), in the present research. Bibliometric analysis has been widely applied in research areas related to extradition, such as terrorism, corruption, money laundering, and cybercrime. For example, Klona et al. There have also been bibliometric studies addressing money laundering, such as that of Dote-Pardo and Severino-González (2025), who mapped challenges in compliance with anti-money laundering efforts in emerging economies. In another study, Zhao and Cheng (2024) investigated research trends in cross- border cybercrime, an increasingly important topic in the field of transnational legal cooperation. Collectively, these studies highlight the usefulness of bibliometric analysis for the scholarly tracing of development with respect to legal issues and related issues. However, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no bibliometric study to date has focused specifically on extradition. This absence limits scholars and practitioners from understanding the broader structure of extradition-related publications and hinders efforts to identify dominant themes or assess knowledge gaps. To address this gap, the present study conducts a bibliometric analysis of the academic literature on extradition published between 2004 and 2024. Bibliometric analysis offers a systematic and evidence-based approach to investigating research development and scholarly impact by analyzing bibliographic data such as publication patterns, citation networks, and keyword trends (Passas, 2024). Bibliometric studies reduce interpretative bias by providing objective and replicable evaluations of research progress, in contrast to systematic literature reviews that rely on qualitative synthesis (Donthu et al., 2021). As a result, they are useful instruments for identifying gaps, tracking collaboration and understanding how knowledge advances in specific domains (Abdullah et al., 2023; Arokiasamy et al., 2024; Huda et al., 2025). 2. Materials and Methods To ensure a clear and organized analysis of the bibliographic data, it is essential to outline the materials and methods used in this study. This improves research consistency, reliability, and transparency (Yuki et al., 2025). In this context, this study adopts the four-step methodology for bibliometric analysis of Öztürk et al. (2024), as outlined below. 2.1. Step 1: Defining the aim of the research Using data from the Scopus database and software tools such as Harzing’s Publish or Perish and VOSviewer, this study aims to map publication trends, document types, productive contributors, highly cited works, and thematic structures in extradition research. Accordingly, the research is guided by the following research questions (RQs): RQ1. What are the trends and current states of publications on extradition? RQ2. Who are the most productive authors, institutions, countries or territories, and source titles in extradition-related publications? RQ3. What are the most frequently cited publications in the field? RQ4. What thematic structures emerge from the analysis of keyword co-occurrence in extradition-related publications? 2.2. Step 2: Collecting data from the relevant literature This study employed the Scopus database, provided by Elsevier, which is currently the largest repository of peer- reviewed abstracts and citations (Wan Mat & Lian, 2025). Scopus indexes a wide range of disciplines (Baas et al., 2020; Alharthi et al., 2023) and is widely recognized as a reliable source for bibliometric research, particularly for identifying research trends and evaluating scholarly impact across various fields (Baas et al., 2020). Its features and functionalities also support bibliometric analysis, making it a suitable and practical choice for this study (Rejeb et al., 2023). On March 23, 2025, a search was carried out to retrieve documents specifically pertaining to extradition by employing the search string TITLE-ABS-KEY (extradition). Using a single keyword in the search is in line with the recommended practices in bibliometric analysis, particularly when the research topic is precise and specific (Donthu et al., 2021; Öztürk et al., 2024). This approach minimized the inclusion of less relevant or unrelated studies and helped ensure that the findings were specifically focused on extradition. The initial search yielded 1,143 documents. Thereafter, several inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to refine the dataset. First, the time frame was limited to 2004-2024. This time frame was selected to reflect the maturity of the research field given that research evaluations are generally more insightful when the subject has attracted a large amount of academic literature (Kraus et al., 2020). Second, for disciplinary focus, the materials in the dataset were restricted to those indexed in the social sciences and arts and humanities. This choice is justified by the fact that extradition is predominantly studied from legal, political, international relations and human rights perspectives. Accordingly, publications from unrelated scientific or technical fields were excluded. Third, only documents in English were included. English is the dominant language of worldwide academic communication (Berdyyev et al., 2025; You et al., 2024) and the main language in Scopus indexing (Vera-Baceta et al., 2019), thus ensuring consistency in keyword analysis and citation interpretation (Berdyyev et al., 2025). Following this screening process, 306 publications were removed. The final dataset contained 837 documents included in the bibliometric https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Masri et al. (2026) 3 analysis. Figure 1 illustrates the document selection process, which adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework (Page et al., 2021). Step 3: Conducting analysis and visualization via bibliometric tools Initially, the data and citation metrics were extracted via Scopus’s built-in Analyze Results feature, which provides an overview of the publication trends, document types, source types, active authors, contributing institutions, and top publishing journals. These data were subsequently exported in two formats: RIS for Harzing’s Publish or Perish and CSV for VOSviewer, along with citation counts, bibliographic data, abstracts, keywords, and funding information. The dual-format export ensures that both tools are compatible and consistent. Harzing's Publish or Perish (version 8) generated detailed citation metrics, such as author impact and citation count, whereas VOSviewer (version 1.6.20) generated and visualized bibliometric maps of keyword co-occurrence. They were selected because of their recognition in the academic community and their capacity to support in-depth bibliometric analysis and research evaluation (Rosmayanti et al., 2024). A combination of these tools produced a complete bibliometric analysis, resulting in the visual mapping presented in the figures and tables in the Results section. 2.4. Interpreting the results to understand research trends and scholarly impact The Discussion section interprets the outputs of bibliometric tools for insights into thematic development, scholarly influence, and trends in extradition research. The Conclusion section expands on the study's implications, limitations and suggestions for future research. 3. Trends and current states of publications The number of publications related to extradition over the past two decades is illustrated in Figure 2, revealing a generally upward trend with several fluctuations. The output volume remained relatively low between 2004 and 2010, with fewer than 20 publications per year. A noticeable increase occurred in 2011, when the number of publications rose to 46. This was followed by a period of moderate activity until 2019. A significant surge began in 2020, with the number of annual publications more than doubling compared with previous years and reaching a peak of 95 documents in 2021. Since then, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Masri et al. (2026) 4 publication levels have remained consistently high, with minor variations, suggesting growing and sustained scholarly interest in extradition-related issues. The data show that journal articles dominate extradition-related publications, comprising 60.69% of the total dataset (508 documents). This is followed by book chapters (21.39%) and review papers (8.48%), which are common formats in legal and social science research. Books represent a smaller share at 6.33%, whereas other formats, such as notes, conference papers, and editorials, together account for less than 5% of the output. The predominance of journal articles reflects the reliance on peer-reviewed discourse to explore extradition, whereas the presence of book chapters and full-length books underscores the enduring value of long-form academic contributions in the field. In the overlay model, the color of each node indicates the average publication year in which the keyword appears. Darker shades represent earlier research focus, whereas lighter or brighter hues denote more recent interest (Digdowiseiso, 2025). In Figure 4, keywords such as extradition, human rights, and European Arrest Warrant appear in darker purple tones, indicating that they were studied earlier in the timeline. The gradient from darker to lighter colors effectively depicts the temporal evolution of research themes in extradition-related publications. This visualization not only maps the thematic connections among keywords but also reveals when these themes became prominent. Moreover, in the density model, color brightness reflects the relative importance and frequency of a keyword’s occurrence in the literature. Brighter areas indicate keywords that appear more frequently and are therefore considered highly significant, whereas darker or faded areas represent keywords that are less common and less central to the research focus (Digdowiseiso, 2025). In contrast, keywords in darker zones, such as identity, umbrella movement, or trade and cooperation agreement, appear less often and represent more niche or emerging areas of study. Discussion The bibliometric findings, institutional patterns, and keyword analysis show how research on extradition has developed over the past two decades. The field has broadened in scope and now engages with a wider range of disciplines and perspectives. Several observations can be drawn from the results. One clear trend is the steady rise of extradition as a topic in academic writing. Interest has been evident since the early 2000s, but the sharp increase in publications after 2020 suggests heightened global awareness. This shift is linked to legal and political events, echoing observations by Chan (2022). Most of the output appears in peer-reviewed journals, signaling alignment with established academic standards. Books and book chapters also feature strongly, indicating demand for more comprehensive, often interdisciplinary, treatments. In contrast, conference papers and editorials are rare, reinforcing the view that extradition is treated as a substantive, theory-driven subject rather than a fast-moving policy debate. Similar trends in the dominance of journal articles have been reported in related bibliometric studies, as highlighted by Patel et al. (2023) and Bui et al. (2021). Another striking feature is the dominance of Hong Kong in the dataset. A significant share of the research has focused on the 2019 anti-extradition bill movement (Cheng, 2020; Cheng et al., 2022; Fong, 2023; Ma & Cheng, 2021; Tang, 2023; Zhu et al., 2022). Even after its withdrawal on 4 September 2019, the bill and events surrounding it have continued to attract scholarly attention (Lee et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Yuen & Mok, 2023). This shows how the social and political context can shape the direction of academic inquiry. While Hong Kong dominates output, work from the United Kingdom, the United States, https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/mr Masri et al. (2026) 10 and other jurisdictions reflects broader international conversation. Together, these contributions combine regional expertise with increasing global engagement. The results also point to an increasingly interdisciplinary approach. Studies linked to the Hong Kong anti-extradition bill protests go well beyond doctrinal legal analysis. They include examinations of digital and social media use (Lee, 2020; Lee & Fong, 2021; Lee et al., 2021b), protest strategies and public reactions (Lee et al., 2021a; Lee et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2024), protest psychology (Li et al., 2024), activism within schools and professional sectors (Ma & Cheng, 2021; Tong & Yuen, 2021), and the influence of diaspora communities (Fong, 2022; Lee, 2022). This range demonstrates how extradition now intersects with communication, political science, sociology, and psychology. Journal patterns also confirm this cross-disciplinary reach, with much of the research published in legal and sociopolitical journals under reputable academic publishers. The most-cited works reveal a balance between long-standing legal scholarship and more recent politically focused analysis. Research on the Hong Kong anti-extradition movement (Lee, 2020; Lee et al., 2019; Purbrick, 2019; Shek, 2020; Ting, 2020) shows how current events can quickly attract academic attention. At the same time, seminal monographs such as Broomhall (2010), Roht-Arriaza (2006), and Schabas (2009) remain influential, reflecting the continuing value of foundational legal research. Finally, the keyword co-occurrence analysis shows that extradition is discussed from legal, political, and human rights perspectives. Common themes include extradition, human rights, and Hong Kong, with related topics such as the European Arrest Warrant and mutual legal assistance. Over the years, the focus has shifted from European legal frameworks to issues raised by the Hong Kong protests. This change confirms the interdisciplinary nature of the field and its responsiveness to broader political developments. Overall, the patterns place extradition firmly at the crossroads of law, human rights, politics, and social activism (Sadoff, 2016; Shum, 2023). 5. Conclusion This study offers insights into the evolution of extradition scholarship across the academic literature by conducting a bibliometric analysis of academic publications on extradition from 2004 to 2024. The analysis mapped research output trends, citation patterns, key contributors, and thematic structures via Scopus-indexed data and tools such as Harzing's Publish or Perish and VOSviewer. The findings demonstrate that extradition has become a subject of sustained scholarly interest, especially since 2019, driven by developments such as protests against the extradition bill in Hong Kong. The analyses show a strong regional focus, significant contributions from Hong Kong, and a clear link to sociopolitical dynamics. This thematic expansion illustrates how the field has matured, shifting from an early emphasis on legal frameworks to a richer, interdisciplinary engagement with political, social, and human rights challenges. The bibliometric evidence also highlights imbalances in regional contributions in which Hong Kong leads substantially, whereas many emerging regions remain underrepresented. Although this bibliometric analysis offers valuable insights, several limitations must be acknowledged. Sole reliance on the Scopus database may have excluded relevant studies from other databases. The decision to employ a single keyword ensured conceptual clarity but may have omitted works framed within broader legal contexts. Furthermore, bibliometric measures reflect academic visibility and not necessarily research quality or societal relevance. To advance the field, future studies could adopt a multi-database approach, broader search strategies, and integrate bibliometric methods with qualitative or quantitative analyses that explore emerging trends, regional perspectives, and ethical implications. Growth in scholarship could be supported by empirical research in underrepresented regions, analysis of new legal and ethical issues, and a stronger social and policy focus addressing the societal repercussions of extradition. Such research could contribute to a more inclusive, forward-thinking scholarly discourse, as legal issues converge with global awareness. Ethical Considerations Not applicable. JSON: Name: extradition_bibliometric_scopus Title: Scopus-based bibliometric analysis to quantify the impact of sociopolitical events on publication and thematic trends in extradition scholarship (2004–2024) Short Hypothesis: The 2019 Hong Kong anti-extradition protests caused a statistically significant increase in the annual rate of extradition-related publications and in mean annual citations per paper in the period 2020–2024 relative to the 2004–2018 baseline. Related Work: Prior work includes domain-specific bibliometric studies that map publication trends, citation networks, and keyword co-occurrence for topics in law, human rights, corruption, terrorism, and cross-border crime. Common methodological components are single-database retrieval (often Scopus), keyword-based corpus construction, descriptive trend analysis, author/institution productivity ranking, citation-count ranking, and network visualization (co-authorship, co-citation, co-occurrence). Limitations in existing approaches are: heavy reliance on a single bibliographic source producing coverage and language bias; narrow or single-keyword search strategies that miss semantically related literature; shallow causal inference linking events to publication changes (typically descriptive before-and-after comparisons without rigorous time-series modelling or control topics); inadequate handling of author and affiliation disambiguation; and limited robustness checks (few multi-database, threshold sensitivity, or ablation studies). These weaknesses constrain claims about event-driven changes, geographic representation, and thematic evolution. Abstract: This research designs and executes a reproducible bibliometric pipeline to test whether a major sociopolitical event—the 2019 Hong Kong anti-extradition protests—caused measurable changes in the volume, citation impact, and thematic composition of extradition scholarship between 2004 and 2024. The approach uses a Scopus-derived corpus constructed with TITLE-ABS-KEY(extradition) and constrained to social sciences and arts & humanities, combined with time-series modelling, interrupted time-series segmented regression, and controlled difference-in-differences analyses against matched legal-topic controls. Visualization and thematic mapping use keyword co-occurrence networks and cluster stability analyses. The main contribution is a rigorously specified experimental protocol that moves beyond descriptive bibliometrics to infer event-associated changes while quantifying sensitivity to database choice, keyword definition, and clustering thresholds. Expected outcomes are statistically validated effect estimates for post-2019 publication and citation changes, robust thematic cluster shifts, and a reproducible pipeline for future event-driven bibliometric evaluations. Experiments: Datasets: primary dataset = Scopus export (metadata, abstracts, author affiliations, keywords, citation counts) retrieved 23-Mar-2025 using TITLE-ABS-KEY(extradition), limited to years 2004–2024, subject areas Social Sciences and Arts & Humanities, language = English (expected N=837). Robustness datasets = Web of Science and Dimensions exports using equivalent query and filters; merged-deduplicated multi-source set. Preprocessing: normalize author names (algorithmic disambiguation), normalize affiliations, deduplicate records across sources using DOI/Title/first-author similarity, extract publication year and document type. Primary outcome variables: annual publication count, annual total citations, mean citations per paper per year, annual publication growth rate. Baselines: (A) pre-event baseline 2004–2018 trend; (B) control-topic baseline using matched legal topics without major 2019 events (e.g., mutual legal assistance or extradition-adjacent terms selected to match 2004–2018 trend via propensity score on pre-2019 trajectory). Statistical analyses: 1) Interrupted time series (ITS) segmented regression on annual counts with breakpoint at 2019, estimating level and slope changes; model family = negative binomial for counts and linear regression for mean citations; report incidence rate ratios (IRR), 95% CIs, p-values. 2) Difference-in-differences (DiD) comparing extradition vs matched control topics, with cluster-robust standard errors. 3) Change-point detection (Bayesian or Pettitt test) as corroboration. 4) Permutation test: random temporal shuffles (n=1000) to estimate distribution under null. Thematic analyses: generate keyword co-occurrence networks using VOSviewer parameters; compute cluster assignments at k=6 and vary minimum-occurrence thresholds (>=3, >=5, >=10) for ablation; compute cluster stability metrics (Adjusted Rand Index) across thresholds and across databases. Baseline comparisons: single-keyword search vs expanded search (TITLE-ABS-KEY(extradition OR "extradit*") vs TITLE-ABS-KEY(extradition)) to quantify corpus sensitivity. Evaluation metrics: effect size (IRR), p-values, change in R-squared/AIC for model fit, Cohen's d for mean-citation changes, ARI for cluster stability, coverage overlap percentage across databases. Ablation studies: (1) exclude Hong Kong-related keywords and rerun ITS/DiD to test locality-driven effects; (2) restrict to journal articles only vs full document set; (3) vary author-disambiguation strictness and measure impact on institution productivity rankings. Reproducibility: provide code, parameter settings, and intermediate exports; pre-register analysis plan before hypothesis testing. Risk Factors and Limitations: Single-database coverage bias: Scopus indexing choices and language coverage may omit regionally published or non-English works, limiting generalizability. Keyword specificity: TITLE-ABS-KEY(extradition) may undercount articles treating extradition implicitly or using alternative terminology, creating false negatives. Temporal citation lag: recently published works (2020–2024) have shorter citation windows, biasing mean-citation comparisons. Confounding events: other synchronous global or regional events may coincide with 2019–2024 trends, limiting causal attribution. Author/affiliation disambiguation errors: misattribution can distort productivity and geographic analyses. Small-sample instability: subgroups (countries, institutions) with few records produce noisy estimates. Bibliometric metrics limitations: citation counts reflect visibility, not quality; network clusters reflect co-occurrence heuristics sensitive to threshold choices. Scalability and compute: merging multiple large bibliographic exports and performing probabilistic disambiguation may require substantial memory/CPU for robustness checks. Legal-discipline heterogeneity: interdisciplinary framing of extradition across political science, sociology, and law complicates consistent subject-area filtering and comparability.
